name: Daria Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the shepherd's helper at High Cairn, a hill farm with about eleven hundred ewes spread over the open hill above Glenmore. In November it's mostly checking the ewes before the rams go in, moving groups between the in-bye fields, which are the walled fields near the house, and the open hill. I'm out on the quad bike by eight with Bess, the young dog, who's about as experienced as I am, which is to say not very.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what did you do before?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eighteen months. Before that I was a care assistant in a nursing home for twenty years, lifting, washing, holding hands at three in the morning. When my partner Jonas got the job as a ranger up here, we moved, and Ines Hallam, who owns High Cairn and is eighty-one, needed someone. She said she'd rather teach a grown woman with a strong back than a boy with a phone, then laughed, because I'm the one always on my phone.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the phone for, out on the hill?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Everything. I use one of the AI apps every day. I photograph a ewe's eye or a sore foot and ask what it might be before I bother Ines, I use it to keep my own notes on which ewe had twins, and it wrote the letter that got us the grant for the new fence. The pay is low, and moving here took every penny we had, so I lean on anything free that makes me better faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, that's more or less where I am already. I'd tell people at the mart, the livestock market in Glenmore, that it's like having a vet student in your pocket who never gets tired of stupid questions. Some of the old men roll their eyes, but a couple have asked me to show them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this picture suits me. I'm behind on skill, I know that, I can't read a ewe's condition by eye the way Ines can. AI as a handy tool is exactly what helps someone like me catch up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it more, and better. I'd build a proper record of every ewe's lambing history from my notes over the winter, so that at scanning time we know who to keep. And I'd run a little evening session in the village hall to show the other hill wives how I use it, for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly. It feels like a ladder I can climb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Give me one moment when the app made a real difference.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last March, three in the morning, a ewe straining with nothing happening, and Ines asleep. I described it and it told me what to feel for, a leg back, that's when one leg is folded the wrong way. I found it, pushed it round, and the lamb came out alive. I cried in the shed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you're careful about with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it gets things wrong, with confidence. Once it told me a lame ewe probably had foot rot when it was a thorn. Now I use it to ask better questions, not to give me answers I don't check.

S0.say: I'd say it's like having a vet student in your pocket who never tires of stupid questions. Some of the older men at the livestock market have asked me to show them.
S0.think: This picture suits me. I'm behind on skill and can't read a ewe by eye like Ines, and a handy tool is exactly what helps someone like me catch up.
S0.do: Builds a proper lambing record for every ewe over the winter so they know who to keep. Runs a free evening session in the village hall to show other hill farm women how she uses AI.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit excited. It feels like a ladder she can climb.
S0.quote: I found it, pushed it round, and the lamb came out alive. I cried in the shed.
S0.fieldNote: Daria is the rare late starter who sees AI as her way of catching up. The lambing story was vivid and showed both her reliance on the tool and her real fear of getting it wrong. She was also clear that the app makes mistakes and that she checks it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the second one. Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should watch who gets left out. Fewer beginners means fewer people like me getting a chance, and I'd say that hill farming already has hardly any young people. I'd say it on the hill farmers' group online, where I'm the noisy one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think slow is fine for me. I'm fifty-eight, I've got maybe seven or eight working years left, and AI will help me more than it replaces me on a hill. What it might replace is the vet calls and the farm advisers, and that could hurt the valley more than us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push Ines to let me take on more, maybe the record keeping for the farm grant scheme, which she hates. I'd try to get a young person from the village in for the lambing season as a paid helper, so at least one beginner gets in. And I'd keep learning, every night, an hour with the books and the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, mostly for the young ones. For me it's more of a quiet green light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it could hurt the valley more than you. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The vet practice in Glenmore has four vets, and if half their calls become an app, maybe they shut and the nearest vet is an hour away. That's fine until you've got a cow calving backwards. I'd be one of the people who made that happen, a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Paying a young helper costs money Ines might not have. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's a hill farm support scheme, public money, that pays part of a trainee's wage. I'd find it and fill in the forms, that's my job now. It's maybe three months of work for one teenager, but it's something.

S1.say: I'd say we should watch who gets left out, because fewer beginners means fewer chances for people like me. Hill farming already has hardly any young people.
S1.think: Slow is fine for me, with seven or eight working years left, and AI will help me more than replace me on a hill. It might replace vets and farm advisers, which could hurt the valley.
S1.do: Takes over the farm grant paperwork from her boss. Finds a public trainee scheme to pay a village teenager to help through lambing, and studies for an hour every night.
S1.feel: Uneasy for the young ones, but for herself it feels like a quiet green light.
S1.quote: That's fine until you've got a cow calving backwards. I'd be one of the people who made that happen, a little.
S1.fieldNote: She surprised me by turning the lens on herself: her own use of AI might help empty the local vet practice. Her answer to fewer beginners was practical, using public money to bring one teenager in. She's progressive but also hands-on about what she can fix.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Third picture. Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say office workers need the same protections we fought for in care work, a union and decent notice. And I'd say the new AI jobs should go to people who lose the old ones, with training paid by the state. I'd post it, and probably argue with my cousin about it at Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's my daughter Mira I'd think of, she does bookings and admin for a travel firm in the city. And Jonas, whose ranger job is half paperwork now. For me, on the hill, it barely touches the ewes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Mira over a video call and go through what her job actually is, task by task, and which parts an assistant could take. Then I'd push her to learn to run those assistants herself, because I've seen how fast you can learn if you're not scared of it. I'd also offer Jonas help moving his paperwork onto the AI so he's out on the hill more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious for Mira, more than I'd show her. But I'd also feel a bit useful, which is a strange thing to feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think Mira would say to her mother telling her to learn AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say, Mum, you learned it to deliver lambs, I'm not a ewe. Then she'd do it anyway, two weeks later, and pretend it was her idea. She's like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'it barely touches the ewes'. Is that really true for your money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not quite, you've caught me. If people in cities have less money, lamb prices drop, and Ines's margin is thin already. So maybe my hours get cut. I hadn't really thought of that until you asked.

S2.say: I'd say office workers need the protections we fought for in care work, a union and decent notice. The new AI jobs should go to the people who lose the old ones, with state-paid training.
S2.think: I'd think of my daughter, who does bookings for a travel firm, and my partner, whose ranger job is half paperwork. On the hill it barely touches the ewes, or so I first thought.
S2.do: Goes through her daughter's job task by task on a video call and pushes her to learn to run the assistants herself. Helps her partner move his paperwork onto AI so he can be outside more.
S2.feel: Anxious for her daughter, more than she'd show, and oddly useful at the same time.
S2.quote: She'd say, Mum, you learned it to deliver lambs, I'm not a ewe.
S2.fieldNote: Her adaptive streak made her a coach for her family rather than a worrier. When I pressed her, she realised lower city spending could cut lamb prices and her hours, which she hadn't considered. She took the correction openly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fourth picture. Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to share it out, through taxes on the people whose shares boom, and put it into public services and the places that never get anything, like hill country. I'd say it at the hall, on the group, wherever. I'd be loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd be squeezed from the side. House prices boom, rich people buy the cottages up here as weekend homes, and Jonas and I rent ours. Ines's nephew already says the farmhouse would fetch a fortune. If she dies, I don't know what happens to High Cairn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Ines, carefully, about what she wants for the farm when she's gone, and whether there's any way it stays a working farm. I'd look into a community buyout, where the village raises money and buys the land together. And I'd use the AI to read every page of the rules on that, because it's thick stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, with a real knot about the farm itself. The job's safe in your picture, but the hill might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: That's a hard conversation with an eighty-one-year-old employer. How would you open it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over tea, after we've sorted the rams, when she's in a good mood. I'd say, Ines, who do you want to be standing here in ten years? She's sharp, she'd know what I meant straight away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you know if a community buyout is realistic here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. I've read about villages doing it, but they had more money than Glenmore. It might be a dream. I'd still want to try before some city bank buys the hill for its trees.

S3.say: I'd say this is the moment to tax the winners and put the money into public services and neglected places like hill country. I'd be loud about it everywhere.
S3.think: I think we'd be squeezed from the side, with weekend-home buyers pushing up prices and us renting. If Ines dies, I don't know what happens to High Cairn.
S3.do: Talks to her elderly boss about her wishes for the farm. Looks into a community buyout, where the village buys the land together, and uses AI to read all the rules.
S3.feel: Anxious, with a knot about the farm itself. The job seems safe, but the hill might not be.
S3.quote: I'd say, Ines, who do you want to be standing here in ten years?
S3.fieldNote: The threat here was land, not jobs: weekend homes and the farm's future after its elderly owner. She was honest that a community buyout might be a dream. Her instinct is still to act, and to use AI to get through heavy rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the last picture. Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots on farms could be good if workers own a share and help decide how they're used. And I'd say loudly that care homes are not warehouses, and I'd fight robots replacing carers, because I know what those hands do. That's where I'd spend my anger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm torn. On the open hill, in sideways rain and bog, I honestly don't know how well a robot does, and nobody knows that yet. But I'm the least skilled person at High Cairn, so if any job goes, it's mine first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be the one who learns the robots, straight away, before anyone else gets the idea. I'd look at drones for gathering sheep and those collars that act as invisible fences, and I'd offer to trial them for free. And I'd ring my old manager at the nursing home to see how my friends there are doing, because they'd be hit hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but buzzing too, which sounds wrong. My job is in danger and my old workmates are in danger, and part of me still wants to get my hands on the controls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the nursing home would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Agnieszka, who I worked nights with for twelve years. She's fifty-five and she knows every resident's tea order and every fear. A robot can lift Mr Daly, but it won't know he only sleeps if you leave the hall light on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're on thin savings. What if the robot trial costs you your job instead of saving it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then at least I'd have learned something people want. I'd rather lose it fighting than lose it waiting. Jonas would say I'm reckless, and he's half right.

S4.say: I'd say farm robots could be good if workers share the gains and the say. And I'd fight robots replacing carers, because I know what those hands do.
S4.think: I'm torn. Nobody knows how well robots cope with sideways rain and bog on an open hill, but I'm the least skilled person at High Cairn, so my job would go first.
S4.do: Volunteers immediately to learn the robots and offers to trial sheep-gathering drones and virtual-fence collars for free. Rings her old nursing home to check on former colleagues.
S4.feel: Alarmed but buzzing, torn between fear for her job and old workmates and an urge to take the controls.
S4.quote: A robot can lift Mr Daly, but it won't know he only sleeps if you leave the hall light on.
S4.fieldNote: Even in the worst picture, she moved first, offering herself as the robot learner. Her strongest feeling was for her old care colleagues, which turned this picture from a farm story into a care story. She admitted honestly she doesn't know how robots would cope on rough hill ground.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The last one, because it comes for the hill and the care homes at once, and those are my two lives. What would help is the workers, and places like Glenmore, owning a slice of the machines, and public money for training people over fifty, not just young ones. Give me a course and a share, and I'll do the rest.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the sheep. Ewes on a hill need someone who notices things. If the robots come, I want rules that say a person still walks the hill, at least at lambing.

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that people assume someone my age is scared of all this. I'm scared of being poor, not of the phone.

headlineQuote: I'm scared of being poor, not of the phone.
portrait: Daria Weber is 58, a former nursing home care assistant who became a shepherd's helper on an 1,100-ewe hill farm eighteen months ago, after moving with her partner Jonas, a ranger. She has almost no savings left after the move and uses an AI app every day to catch up on skills she knows she lacks, once to save a lamb at three in the morning. She sees the early pictures as a ladder, worries next for her daughter's office job and for the hill farm's future in a house price boom, and in the robot picture is both alarmed and eager to take the controls. Her deepest anger is for her old care colleagues if robots arrive in nursing homes.
biggestWorry: The robot picture worries her most, because it hits both hill farming and care work, her two working lives.
whatWouldHelp: Workers and rural communities owning a share of the machines, and public money to train people over fifty. She also wants a rule that a person still walks the hill at lambing.
